questions.question: Which document is the best semantic match for this query?
questions.query: How can I fix a car that will not start?

options.text: Motorcycle engine maintenance tips for beginners
Troubleshooting an automobile that will not turn on
Car seat cleaning tips for leather interiors

correct.title: B is the best semantic match.
why_correct: automobile ≈ car  (synonyms for the same vehicle type)
will not turn on ≈ will not start  (same failure concept)
why_others: A (motorcycle maintenance): shares the vehicle-repair domain, but motorcycle ≠ car and maintenance ≠ fixing a starting failure
C (car seat cleaning): shares the surface word "car" but the topic is cleaning, not repair

incorrect.title: The correct answer is B.

review.heading: If you chose A (motorcycle maintenance):
review.body: This is a strong distractor! Motorcycles and cars are both motor vehicles, and maintenance is related to repair. But semantic search looks at the full intent: the query is about a car that will not start, while option A is about general motorcycle upkeep. The meaning is close but not the best match.

review.heading: If you chose C (car seat cleaning):
review.body: "Car" appears in both, but keyword overlap is exactly the trap! Cleaning is a different task from fixing a starting problem.

incorrect.summary: B works because "automobile ≈ car" and "will not turn on ≈ will not start" — the meaning aligns even though the wording differs.

questions.question: Why did keyword search rank the irrelevant shoe-brands document first in the puppy example?

options.text: Because the most relevant document used related words (slippers, biting) instead of exact query words (shoes, chewing)
Because semantic search always prefers longer documents
Because keyword search ignores nouns and only looks at verbs

correct.title: A is correct.
why_correct: Keyword search counts exact word matches. The shoe-brands doc matched on "shoe," while the actually helpful Doc A used synonyms: slippers ≈ shoes | biting ≈ chewing | dogs ≈ puppy
Keyword search cannot recognize these meaning links, so it over-valued the surface match ("shoe brands") and missed the best answer.
Semantic search captures this synonymy because embeddings place related concepts close together in meaning space.

incorrect.title: The correct answer is A.

review.heading: If you chose B ("semantic search prefers longer documents"):
review.body: Document length is not what drives semantic ranking. Semantic search scores meaning similarity regardless of how long a passage is.

review.heading: If you chose C ("keyword search ignores nouns"):
review.body: Keyword search does count nouns — that is exactly why "shoe" in the brands doc earned a high ranking. The problem is that keyword search can only see exact surface words, not synonyms or related concepts.

incorrect.summary: The real issue: the best document used slippers instead of shoes and biting instead of chewing. Keyword search has no way to know these are equivalent, so it ranked the wrong doc first.
